At one banquet, this man allegedly mistook a fish for a man whose execution he had ordered. This man said of a deceased rival that there "wasn't a bone in this wretched fellow," and this ruler ended the tenure of the anti-pope Laurentius by supporting Symmachus. This king ordered the construction of the Basilica of Saint Apollinaris and patronized the scholar Cassiodorus. After this husband of Audofleda died, his daughter Amalasuntha held power until she was murdered in her bath, and this victor at the battles of Isonzo and Verona also ordered the death of the author of Consolation of Philosophy, Boethius. After winning a campaign at the behest of Emperor Zeno, this man stabbed Odoacer to death at a banquet. Name this "great" Ostrogoth king who ruled from Ravenna after the fall of the Roman Empire.

Before this event, Alexander Friedman sent a telegram reading "Mr. Amos kept his promise from the fifth-third." Tosia Altman died in a factory fire during this event, and Samuel Zygielbojm committed suicide in London to protest the British reaction to this event. A mass suicide at 18 Mila Street was carried out by members of the ZOB during this event, and David Appelbaum, the leader of the ZZM was killed during it. A report on this event claimed that its central location "Was No More," and that report was issued by a man who blew up blocks of houses during this event, Jurgen Stroop. After this event, many of its surviving participants were deported to Treblinka. Name this uprising against the Nazis undertaken by Jewish inhabitants of a certain ghetto.

The December 20th Movement was founded by supporters of this man after his removal from power. Eric Delvalle was one of the "Kleenex Presidents" who served under this ruler, whose forces assassinated Hugo Spadafora. Condemnation of this man's regime heightened after a photo of this man's Dignity Battalions beating a bloody Billy Ford was widely circulated. Succeeded by Guillermo Endara, Maxwell Thurman led the military operation that overthrew this man, Operation Just Cause. After being trapped in the Vatican Embassy, this man was played Metallica and Howard Stern Show clips before surrendering to US forces. Name this CIA collaborator and convicted cocaine trafficker, who ruled Panama from 1983 to 1989.

According to one scholar, a traitor to one side of this battle coughed up a tooth to fulfill a prophecy prior to this engagement. This battle is depicted on a sarcophagus in Brescia that was heavily copied from the Painted Colonnade. The losing side made a last stand near the "Great Marsh" and the winning side spread out and charged, eliminating the losing side's superior archers and cavalry. The 192 soldiers lost by the winning side is commemorated by a mound named the Soros. That side had one of their commanders, Callimachus, perish at this battle and the losing side's commander had previously replaced Mardonius. That man, Datis, had his taxis destroyed by hoplites under Miltiades. Name this battle, a Greek victory over the Persians, after which Pheidippides ran a lot to tell Athens about the win.

During one attack on this city, Catherine Cheynel allegedly poured boiling soup on the invaders. This city was the subject of a letter by Cardinal Jacopo Sadoleto, and the capture of this city was the object of the Fraternity of the Spoon. The Escalade festival celebrates Charles Emmanuel of Savoy's failure to take this city. This city, the home of libertine groups like the Spirituels and Patriots, was the site of a revolt led by Ami Perrin. William Farel was a minister in this city where the anti-trinitarian Michael Servetus was burnt at the stake. One leader of this city established a Consistory of twelve elders here with his Ecclesiastical Ordinances. Name this city once ruled by the author of Institutes of the Christian Religion, John Calvin.

This man's name derives from an eagle seen before his birth, and a hyacinth spelling out the first two letters of his name grew on the spot where he perished. Eurysaces, this man's son by his concubine Tecmessa, succeeded this man's father as king of Salamis. This man killed himself after an episode in which he slaughtered a bunch of sheep while he was angry over losing out on some armor forged by Hephaestus. Earlier, this hero helped retrieve the body of Achilles, and twice nearly crushed Hector with huge rocks. Name this strong son of Telamon, the greater of two Greek heroes with the same name.

This man absolved his herald Copreus of the murder of the Elean Iphitus. Following his death, this husband of Antimache was succeeded by his uncles Atreus and Thyestes as king of Tiryns. Hera hastened the labor of his mother Alcippe due to a prophecy that the first of Perseus's descendents to be born would take the throne. After his uncle Electryon was killed, this man's father Sthenelus banished Amphitryon. This man signaled his cowardice by repeatedly hiding in a large bronze urn after seeing the Cretan Bull and the corpse of the Nemean Lion. Name this Mycenaean king who directed the twelve Labors of Hercules.

Ares killed Halirrhothius, who attempted to rape this man's granddaughter Alcippe. He invented funeral rites, barley cakes for sacrifices, and monogamy. Hermes bribed this man's wife Aglauros in order to rape this man's daughter Herse. He discovered at Delphi that his city needed to decide a heavenly contest after he observed the growth of the first olive tree. Despite the fact that he succeeded his father in law Antaeus as king, he is often considered the first king of Athens. Identify this possibly semi-historic king of Athens whose body was half-serpent.

When Jason stayed in Maenalus, this woman gave him a spear. This woman's only son carried a shield bearing an image of a Sphinx carrying a Theban man when that son attacked the 5th gate of Thebes. This mother of Parthenopaeus killed the centaurs Rhaecus and Hylaeus, who tried to rape her. She was nursed by a bear sacred to Artemis, and Zeus turned her into a lion to prevent her from sleeping with Melanion, who married her after using golden apples to distract her during a race. Meleager fell in love with what woman while they were both hunting the Calydonian Boar?

This man's paternal grandfather Sigi killed a man named Bredi who outdid him in a hunt. This man was conceived after his mother ate a golden apple carried by the giantess Hljod, whom this man later married. Nine of this man's sons were killed by a wolf that was actually the shapeshifting mother of this man's killer. He died while visiting his son-in-law, a king of Gautland named Siggeir who was present in this man's home when Odin placed a sword in the Barnstokk. Name this father of Signy and Sigmund, the namesake of a Norse saga.

When Talthybius called for this woman to be brought to him, she was found praying to Hymen. Eurypylus went mad upon seeing an image of Dionysus hidden in a chest left behind by this woman. In one myth, her ears were licked by serpents after she spent a night in a temple of Apollo. A wooden carving of Athena fell to the ground when this woman was raped, and Odysseus called for the stoning of her rapist, Ajax the Lesser. When this woman refused Apollo's advances, he spat in her mouth. Clytemnestra killed this woman after Agamemnon brought her home from the Trojan War. Identify this daughter of Priam and Hecuba, who was not believed when she claimed that Greek soldiers were in the Trojan Horse.

Apollodorus says that a son of Zeus and Niobe with this name was the grandfather of Io, and the namesake of a city first ruled by Phoroneus. Another man of this name was the eldest son of Chalciope and Phrixus; that man gives a speech urging Jason to go to the river Ister in a work by Apollonius Rhodius. A third figure of this name is described as an adept hunter of deer and goats, and was the first to recognize Odysseus when he returned to Ithaca. One figure of this name was lulled to sleep and slain by Hermes while he was guarding Io, a task in which he made use of the eyes all over his body. Give this name also shared by the man who built the ship in which Jason and his companions sailed.

Trygaeus once said that a beetle from this place would serve as a boat for him. Acoestus sacrificed to Dionysus upon reaching this place after being the only one out of twenty pirates who was not turned into a dolphin, after Acoestus's shipmates brought Dionysus to Asia instead of sailing him to this "vine-leaf shaped" island. On this island with "maenad-haunted hills," Artemis turned into a deer and ran between Otus and Ephialtes, causing them to kill each other. Dionysus begat Staphylus and Oenopion by a Cretan princess whom he rescued on this island. Identify this Greek island on which Theseus abandoned Ariadne.

He's not Lleu Llaw Gyffes, but this figure resembled a jellyfish when he was born, so his mother wrapped him in a lock of her hair and threw him into the sea. He took the shape of a wood pigeon to descend to the Underworld, which was ruled by his father, and he tricked a goddess into discarding her burning fingernails, thus learning from her that wood can be used to make fire. A flock of birds woke up the goddess of death while this figure was trying to gain immortality by crawling into her body. His other deeds include using his sister's hair to lasso the sun and force it to move slower, and hauling up the North Island while fishing. Name this Polynesian trickster hero who is the namesake of a Hawaiian island.

Because Oeneus had entertained this man for twenty days and gave him a purple belt, Diomedes made peace with Glaucus during the Trojan War. This son of Eurymede earned his best-known name when he killed a tyrant of Corinth. This man sacrificed a white bull to Poseidon, following instructions from a dream in which Athena brought him a golden bridle. He was ambushed by a group of Lycians sent by Iobates, who had earlier protected this man despite a letter sent by Proetus ordering Iobates to kill this man. He died on the Aleian plain after his mount was stung by a gadfly during an attempt to ascend Mount Olympus. Identify this man who slew the Chimaera while mounted on Pegasus.

According to legend, Harald Bluetooth forced Palnatoki to demonstrate his proficiency with this item on his son. Another one of these items partially made of ivory was given to Orestes in an attempt to protect him from the Furies. In the Ramayana, King Janaka breaks one belonging to Shiva given to him by Parasurama, and in the Mahabharata Karna was killed with one of these weapons, which was called the Gandiva. During the Trojan War, Diomedes and Odysseus went to Lemnos to retrieve one these weapons wielded by Philoctetes. Name this weapon wielded by Arjuna, which Heracles used to shoot projectiles dipped in the blood of the Hydra.

This man received bread from the satyr Silenus in exchange for wine from Maron. A variant myth claims that this man's son Romanus colonized Rome. While avenging the death of Leukos, this man accidentally killed Demokoön. He struck Thersites after Thersites insulted Agamemnon, and he buried some gold and forged a letter from Priam to frame a son of Nauplius. King Alcinous of the Phaiakians briefly sheltered this man, whose rival Palamedes proved that this man was faking insanity by throwing his infant son in front of his plow. Identify this son of Laertes who was seduced by Calypso, and who, with the help of Eumaeus and Telemachus, killed the suitors of his wife Penelope.

According to Pindar, this event was triggered when a native of Pallene or Phlegra stole the cattle of Helios. A prophecy about this event led Zeus to grope about in search of an invincibility herb after he ordered the Sun and Moon to stop shining. The prophecy about this event also mentioned needing a "lion-skinned mortal," so Athena went off to recruit Heracles, who had to carry Alcyoneus out of Phlegra in order to kill him. Mount Ossa was piled on Mount Pelion by Otus and Ephialtes during this battle. Name this struggle between the Olympians and some children of Tartarus and Gaia, a sequel to the Titanomachy.

Pelias mistakenly expected this father of Bucolion to prevent the Argonauts from passing the Hellespont and reaching the Euxine. Phoenodamas persuaded this man to sacrifice his daughter, but she became Telamon's concubine and bore this man's grandson Teucer after being rescued by Heracles. This father of Tithonus had a son who was known as Podarces until he was ransomed by this man's daughter Hesione. Apollo and Poseidon were forced to serve this man, for whom they built the Scaean Gates. Name this Trojan king, the father of Priam, who owned a pair of immortal horses that he refused to give to Heracles.

This man sported a Tegean blade and a panther skin and was accompanied by twin guard dogs. His mother formed many of the characters of the Latin alphabet, and he first introduced that alphabet to Italy. His ally's father gave this man a quiver and a cloak with golden threads. After this son of Carmentis gave a speech promising the aid of four hundred horsemen, an omen of thunder was sent by Venus for her son, whom this man had earlier given a tour of his kingdom. Vergil claims this king laid Rome's cornerstone, and he hosted Hercules while he was defeating Cacus. Identify this Arcadian king who, while in Italy, offered his son Pallas as military aid to Aeneas.

This man moved to Northumbria after his younger brother gave him a gold ring in recompense for his share of a kingdom, according to The Saga of King Hrolf Kraki. In a different source, this man gives his daughter in marriage in an attempt to prevent a blood feud after the slaying of Froda, but Froda's son Ingeld eventually starts a battle against him. Men under the command of this husband of Wealtheow include Unferth, who lends the sword Hrunting to a hero who visits this ruler. Name this king of the Scyldings who built the hall Heorot and asked Beowulf to kill Grendel.

Some sources state that this man led a failed raid on Cichyrus, but was captured by Aidoneus and killed by Aidoneus's hound. His sister Theisadie accompanied Helen to Troy years after this Thessalian lost a drawing of lots which could have given him Helen as a wife. Mopsus recognized a bird as the soul of Caeneus after he died at an event hosted by this man, which devolved into a battle for Mount Pelion. Most sources state that this man wound up bound to a Chair of Forgetfulness after he audaciously traveled to Hades in an attempt to take Persephone as his wife. Name this friend of Theseus whose earlier wedding to Hippodameia was disrupted when his Centaur guests began fighting his Lapith subjects.

Antipoenus's daughters Androcleia and Alcis died to ensure that this city would be safe from the forces of the Minyan king Erginus. This city's forces fought the Sicyonian king Epopeus during the reign of Nycteus. Two kings of this city avenged the mistreatment of their mother Antiope at the hands of Dirce, and built this city's walls. Those two kings, one of whom could move boulders by playing a lyre, were Zethus and Amphion. Attacks on this city were led by a group that included Tydeus and Adrastus, and later by the Epigoni, after which Creon's son abdicated. Name this city founded by Cadmus that was later ruled by Laius and Oedipus.

This man defeated Immardus in a battle with the Eleusians. When Eumolpus attacked his city, this man defeated him after gaining divine favor by sacrificing his youngest daughter, which led his other daughters to commit suicide in sympathy with her death. As an infant, this husband of the Naiad Praxithea, or his grandfather of the same name, was placed by Athena in a basket guarded by two snakes; a peek into the basket resulted in the suicides of the daughters of Cecrops. Identify this man, conceived when Athena wiped Hephaestus' semen off her leg onto the ground, a legendary early king of Athens.

Harpalyce got Clymenus to take this action, and this was done to Itys by Tereus. After she had torn out her eyes in grief, Lamia began to do this. Zeus killed a group of Titans who smeared themselves with gypsum before doing this, after which Athena implanted a statue with the heart of Zagreus. Aerope's husband avenged her seduction by forcing Thyestes to do this. While mourning for Persephone, Demeter absentmindedly began to do this, leading Hephaestus to make a replacement shoulder of ivory for Pelops after the banquet of Tantalus. Identify this action, the primary reason for the curse on the house of Atreus, a fate that Zeus escaped when Rhea gave a rock to Cronus.

In Ly Myreur des Histors, this figure was buried alive in the tomb of a woman whose corpse he cannibalized, and died of starvation instead of in battle. Other sources state that this foster son of Nabor survived a shipwreck meant to kill all noble children born on May Day. Early sources called him the husband of Cywyllog, and said that his parents were Anna and Lot. He and his half-brother Agravain exposed Guinevere's affair with Lancelot, and in some sources this man tries to seduce Guinevere and claim the throne. Name this treacherous son of Morgause who killed and was killed by King Arthur.

This man captured two demigods by mixing wine and honey with water, then learned a charm for thunder and lightning involving onions, human hair, and sardines. This man added the month of Mercedinus to the calendar, and repealed a law which allowed fathers to sell their sons. An item that descended from heaven into this man's hands during a famine was copied eleven times by Mamarius, and the resulting twelve Ancilia were guarded by the Salii, a group of priests he founded. Prior to his reign, 150 senators shared the rule of Rome, ruling for six hours each. This Sabine was born on the day of the founding of Rome, and he disbanded the Celeres, the guards of Romulus. Name this founder of the Vestal Virgins who was Rome's second king.

The fork in the road at which Oedipus killed Laius led to Daulia and to this place. This place was the site of a temple built by two brothers who rested for six days and then were rewarded by dying on the seventh day after finishing construction. In addition to a temple designed by the architects Agamedes and Trophonius, this place was home to the rock that Rhea disguised as Zeus, which landed here after Cronus spit it out. The goddess Themis presided here until Python was slain. Identify this center of prophecy, the location of a famous oracle taken over by Apollo.

He won the Jugerthine War, but he did not get the name Numidicus. He was the first man to hold 7 consulships, but he is not Augustus. He launched the first proscription, but he is not Sulla. In fact, he was Sulla's opponent. FTP., who defeated the Germans, but proved a better general than politician, like his nephew Gaius Julius Caesar?

In Dec. 1914, hostilities from WWI stretched to the far ends of the globe at this battle between Von Spee and a British squadron under Admiral Sturdee. The Germans lost 4 of their 5 ships, including the commander, Von Spee. FTP, what was this naval engagement, a resounding victory for Britain, fought off the shore of British islands in the South Atlantic?

In 1959, the German Social Democratic Party adopted the Bad Godesberg manifesto of principles, in which it renounced orthodox Marxism for socialism via the ballot box. This was 60 years after this man advocated such a path, causing a serious rift in the SDP. A friend of Engels, he discovered by research that late 19th century economic trends in Europe diverged from Marxist predictions, and published his results in "Evolutionary Socialism." FTP, name this German theoretician who argued that socialism was not predetermined to succeed capitalism.

With a Rooster as a mascot, this faction opposed the ultimate nominee of the Democratic Party in 1848 over the slavery issue. Their refusal to support Lewis Cass gave Zachary Taylor the election. Their common nickname came from the charge that they were willing to torch the house, rather than allow their ideological opponents to stay on board. FTP, what is the flamboyant nickname of this group which supported Martin Van Buren?

This single-screw sloop of war commanded by Captain John Semmes embarked on a 23-month, 75,000 mile voyage in August of 1862; during that time, it never stopped at a port in its home country. The cruise ended when it was sunk outside the port of Cherbourg, France, in 1864 but by then it had burned 53 Union merchantmen and captured nine more. FTP, what was this ship, built and outfitted in Birkenhead, England, which gave its name to an Anglo-American dispute following the Civil War?

She has called herself a Christian mystic with an audience of primarily agnostic nonbelievers.' Her works include 'Tickets at a Prayer Wheel,' 'Holy the Firm,' and most recently 'The Writing Life.' FTP, name this American poet and essayist, winner of the 1974 Pulitzer Prize for 'Pilgrim at Tinker Creek.'

It is made up of 250,000 square miles of dry, hot, wind-swept sand dunes. Pretty useless, you'd think, but try to tell that to the inhabitants of this Arabic monarchy, who found bubblin' crude (oil, that is) under all that sand. FTP, w hat is this enormous desert, whose name translates to 'Empty Quarter?'

Born in 1586, this minister fled to Holland from the Church of St. Mary in Chelmsford, England, and in 1633 left for Massachusetts Bay Colony, for being too much of a Puritan for the prevailing tastes. A group of his Cambridge follower s and he left when he suggested that non-Church members should be allowed to vote. For this he has been called the 'Founder of American Democracy.' FTP, name this man who founded the city of Hartford.

The sponsor of this 1862 act served a then record 42 years in Congress. It granted each state a portion of the public domain in proportion to its congressional representation. Intended to stimulate agriculture by providing training f or farmers, it led to the establishment of large state universities around the country. FTP, name this act which helped start the A & M schools.

One of the leaders in the 1960's and 70's in the movement to free art from the confines of the gallery system, he was pre- occupied with what he termed 'the dialectic between the site and non-site.' FTP, name this Earth-Works artist, best known for his monumental works such as Amarillo ramp, the project he died working on, and Spiral Jetty.

- 20 -10 Up on your economic history? For a possible thirty points, name this economist from the clues. 30: Some of his early works were The Economic Theory of Women's Dress and The Barbarian Stautus of Women. Whether or not these were inspired by his wife, the niece of the president of his alma mater, we will never know. 20: Born in Wisconsin to Norwegian immigrants, this intriguing character was known to wear a coonskin cap to formal events. He apparently was not as concerned with status as were the subjects of his most famous works. 10: Author of Theory of the Leisure Class, this Carleton College alumnus provided an early harbinger to the conspicuous consumption of the eighties.

His first mistake was to deflower royal maid-of-honor Bessy Throckmorton, an act which led to his first stay in the Tower of London. His last mistake was his hare-brained private invasion of the Guyanas, which exhausted the limited patience of James I and led to his 1618 beheading. The legend of his spreading a cloak over a puddle so that the queen may cross dry shod is mentioned in Kenilworth. FTP, name this historian and adventurer whose most famous failure was the lost colony of Roanoke.

According to legend, he was a 17th-century owner of a rent-a-horse business, whose stable contained both fast and not-so-fast horses. When allowed to pick, his customers always took the fast ones, and for some reason, this greatly bothered him. So he instituted a new system of assigning horses, under which each customer would have exactly two choices: he could take the horse nearest the wall, or he could take no horse at all. FTP, name this man who thus lent his name to a type of choice that is not really a choice at all.

He began his education at a state school for defective children and completed it at the London School of Economics, from which he graduated without ever taking a course in economics. He still had no formal economic training by 1932, when, as a professor at Dundee, he first developed the theories that he would later publish as The Nature of the Firm. FTP, name this University of Chicago economist whose landmark 1961 article "The Problem of Social Cost" helped win him a 1991 Nobel Prize.

The Mormayer of Moray, he married Gruoch, a granddaughter of Kenneth II. A grandson of Malcolm II, he was noted for his piety, and in 1050, he became the first monarch in his nation's history to make a pilgrimage to Rome. Although his reign as a whole was unusually peaceful, it ended in violence at the 1057 battle of Lumphanan, where he was killed by the future Malcolm III, the son of his murdered predecessor Duncan. FTP, name this Scottish king, best known as the protagonist of a Shakespeare tragedy.

In Greek, this word literally means "on the threshhold of the bridal chamber," and in Roman literature, it was the name of a poetic genre whose greatest practitioner was Catullus. In English literature, it is better known as the title of a single poem, written to celebrate the author's 1594 marriage to Elizabeth Boyle. FTP, name this work by Edmund Spenser.

For most of his life, he was considerably less famous than his father-in- law, Massachusetts Chief Justice Lemuel Shaw, a judge who is still considered one of the nation's most influential common-law jurists. In addition, it was Shaw's generosity that saved his family after 1857, when the failures of Pierre and Confidence-Man had ruined his career as a writer. FTP, name this novelist, who during his lifetime was most famous for the early novels Typee and Mardi.

It began as an association of law students who felt that all social changes since the eighth century were misguided and sinful, and it later became notable for its fierce opposition to all forms of art, music, and luxury. Operating from their base in Dar'iyya, they had conquered most of their region by 1800, and in the early twentieth century they spearheaded the revolt against Ottoman rule. FTP, name this religious and military sect of the Arabian peninsula, whose leaders founded the modern state of Saudi Arabia.

Although the Council of Jerusalem had ruled that non-Jewish converts to Christianity did not need to be circumcised, many churches in remote areas ignored this edict. Accordingly, one of these churches soon drew a reprimand, which set out a defense of official church teaching and a theory of why Christ made the Mosaic law obsolete. FTP, name this Epistle of Paul, which is named for a people of inner Anatolia.

This holding company was created by Oakes Ames, who, like most of its other stockholders, was a member of Congress, and its only real function was to skim federal grant money away from the Union Pacific corporation. FTP, name either this dummy corporation or its namesake scandal, which arose out of the building of the transcontinental railroad.

His troubles with his country's authoritarian rulers date back to his early satires _A Dance of the Forests_ and _Kongi's Harvest_, and in 1967 he was imprisoned for sympathizing with a secessionist uprising. It was while in prison that he produced some of his best work, including the poetry collection _Shuttle in the Crypt_ and the novel _The Man Died_. FTP, name this exiled poet, playwright, and Yoruba folklorist, who in 1986 became the first black African to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.

Celebrated on September 29, this saint was regarded in the Middle Ages as the presiding spirit of the planet Mercury. He is represented with scales in the final judgment, with which he weighs the souls of the dead. He is mentioned as the guardian angel of Israel in the Bible. FTP, name this prince of angels and leader of the celestial armies.

He first gained attention by winning the Prix de Rome for "L'Enfant prodigue", a cantata. He eventually sacrificed his influence from Richard Wagner for an innovative impressionist style, as in such works as "Feux d'artifice" and "Children's Corner". FTP, name this French composer, whose Suite Bergamasque includes the famous "Clair de lune".

The court ruled in this case that Tennessee citizens were denied equal protection under the 14th amendment by "arbitrary and capricious" malapportionment; overrepresentation of rural districts in state legislatures had disfranchised millions of voters. FTP, name this 1962 case which led to the doctrine of "one man, one vote".

The title character is a US Naval officer involved in treason with Aaron Burr. His expressed desire never to hear the name of his country again is carried out. And for 55 years, he goes from 1 vessel to another in exile, never permitted to be reminded of the United States in print or conversation. FTP, what is this novel featuring the character Philip Nolan by Edward Everett Hale?

He was born in NYC in 1793 but represented Louisiana in the US House and Senate just prior to the Civil War. Prior to the Mexican War he was sent to the Mexican government to discuss Mexican-US differences and the shabby treatment he received was one cause of the war. It was in another diplomatic role, as Confederate commissioner to France in the Trent affair, that he is most famous. For 10 points name this Confederate commissioner to France.

In 19th century Sicily, Lola is married to Alfio but is having an affair with the soldier Turiddu. According to the code of honor of the village Alfio must revenge himself on Turiddu, and he does this by challenging Turiddu to a duel and killing him. This describes the action in, what opera by Pietro Mascagni?

After a successful engineering career, he won international reputation during World War I when he served as chairman of the American Relief Committee, chairman of the Commission for Relief in Belgium, and U.S. Food Administrator. From 1921-1928 he served as secretary of commerce and found the time to write American Individualism. FTP, identify this person who, in 1928, defeated Al Smith for the presidency?

One of the great mysteries of modern history has been solved: William Tager said this phrase. In 1994 Tager shot and killed an NBC employee. Apparently Tager is mentally disturbed and thinks that the media have him under surveillance and beam hostile messages at him. Thus this question to Dan Rather while he was beating Rather up was an effort to stop these transmissions. For 10 points what did Tager ask Rather that night?

He was born in London in 1573 and served as surveyor, or architect, to James I and Charles I. He made influential costumes and sets for plays presented to the English court but is best known as the first major architect of the English Renaissance. After studying the work of Palladio he brought the Palladian style to England, and his most famous building is the Banqueting House. For 10 points name this English architect.

His career started out as a stagehand in a traveling theatrical troupe. When the group disbanded he was forced to work in a flour mill, during which time he wrote 130 plays, 21 of which still survive. Through his plays, he introduced to the non-Greek world such characters as the braggart soldier in his Miles Gloriosus and the sly servant in his Pseudolus. FTP, who was this person, considered the greatest comic playwright of Rome?

The Frenchman Montbar "The Exterminator" and Peter Dieppe "The Great" were noted ones. But the most famous of them was Henry Morgan, who in 1670 marched across the Isthmus of Panama and plundered Panama City after a desperate battle. FTP, what was this association of pirates who ravaged the Caribbean Sea during the 16th and 17th century which shares its name with a professional football team in Tampa, Florida?

Her lover, Mario Cavaradossi, is being tortured for concealing a political prisoner. So she reveals the location of the prisoner to Scarpia, the chief of police. Scarpia then offers to release Mario if this title character will give herself to him. She agrees, but stabs Scarpia at the last moment. Mario dies and she commits suicide. FTP, who is this heroine, the title character in an opera by Puccini?

After dropping out of Harvard, he went to Kenyon to study with John Crowe Ransom. He served jail time for being a conscientious objector to World War II, and his manic-depressive behavior is often the subject of his work. At the time of his death in 1977, like so many of his family predecessors, he was one of the most influential poets of his generation. Identify, FTP, the author of "Skunk Hour" and "For the Union Dead."

Seymour is dead. Buddy is a college writing professor who used to be a panelist on the radio quiz show "Wise Children." The female title character is seeking to learn how to pray incessantly, and her older brother, the male in the title, attacks her with vicious cynicism. Identify this 1961 best- seller, J. D. Salinger's novel about two members of the Glass family.
